slides.title: Multi-Step Equations
slides.note: Post the learning target. Say one line and nothing else yet: “Today: multi-step equations with fractions and decimals.”

slides.title: Warm-Up
slides.note: Q4 is today's move in miniature: two-thirds of 9 is 6, so two-thirds of 9x is 6x. Say that in one sentence after the reveal — Notes II and board 2 distribute a negative fraction the same way. Two minutes silent, then reveal, no discussion.

slides.title: Warm-Up
slides.note: Reveal. Ask for the band each question came from only if time allows.

slides.title: Vocabulary
slides.sub: The new words, before they are used.
slides.note: Two words for today's numbers. A common denominator is the number that clears every fraction at once — 6 for halves and thirds, 15 for thirds and fifths. A rational coefficient is just a fraction or a decimal in front of the variable; the moves of the last three days do not change.

slides.title: Notes
slides.note:
The order of the last three days, every move on its own line: distribute on both sides (6x − 12 + 5 and 2x + 12 + 1); collect each side (6x − 7 and 2x + 13); take 2x from both sides (4x − 7 = 13); add 7 (4x = 20); divide by 4. Check in both sides of the first equation: 3(6) + 5 = 23 and 2(11) + 1 = 23.
OFF: 'Distribute, collect, take the same term from both sides, divide, check. Every equation, every time.'

slides.title: Notes
slides.note:
The fraction multiplies every term inside, just as a whole number does — and a negative fraction carries its sign to each term, as 11.01's −3 did: (−½)(4x) = −2x and (−½)(−10) = +5. Then add 2x to both sides (the smaller x-term is −2x), add 1, divide by 3. Check: −½(8 − 10) = 1 and 2 − 1 = 1. A board with −2x − 10 sent the fraction to one term; one with −2x − 5 lost the sign. Fractions can also be CLEARED — multiply every term by a common denominator — and that is Example 2.
OFF: 'A fraction outside the parentheses multiplies every term inside — sign and all.'

slides.title: Notes
slides.note:
The state's own shape: a negative decimal outside, a decimal left over. −2.4 times 5x is −12x; −2.4 times −3 is +7.2 — not a whole number, and that is fine. Subtract 7.2 from both sides: −12x = −48. Divide by −12: x = 4. Check: −2.4(20 − 3) = −2.4(17) = −40.8. This is the skill the state scored lowest on its released Grade 8 test — almost four in five students missed it — and the miss is nearly always the decimal never reaching the second term (−12x − 3) or its sign (−12x − 7.2).
OFF: 'The decimal is a number like any other. It multiplies every term inside, sign and all.'

slides.title: Example 1
slides.sub: A decimal outside, the variable on both sides.
slides.note: Ask what 0.2 of 10x is, and what 0.2 of −15 is, before anyone writes.

slides.title: Example 1
slides.note: 0.2 of 10x is 2x; 0.2 of −15 is −3 — both terms. Take x (the smaller) from both sides: x − 3 = 4. Add 3: x = 7. Check in both sides of the first equation: 0.2(55) = 11 and 7 + 4 = 11. A board with x = 19 wrote 2x − 15 (the decimal to one term only); one with x = 1 wrote 2x + 3 (the sign).

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.sub: Same steps, your numbers. Boards up when done.
slides.note: 0.6 of 10x is 6x and 0.6 of −5 is −3: 6x − 3 = 4x + 5. Take 4x: 2x − 3 = 5, so 2x = 8 and x = 4. Check: 0.6(35) = 21 and 4(4) + 5 = 21. A board with x = 5 wrote 6x − 5 (the decimal to one term only); one with x = 1 wrote 6x + 3 (the sign).

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.note: Reveal; name what a wrong board most likely did (see the note above).

slides.title: Example 2
slides.sub: Clear the fractions with a common denominator.
slides.note: Ask what number both 2 and 3 divide into, before anyone writes: 6. Then ask which terms the 6 must multiply: all four.

slides.title: Example 2
slides.note: Halves and thirds clear with 6. The second line is the one students skip: 6 multiplies EVERY term — the 3 and the 5 as well as the fractions. 6 times x/2 is 3x; 6 times 3 is 18. A board with 3x + 3 = 2x + 5 multiplied only the fractions (x = 2).

slides.title: Example 2
slides.note: No fractions are left: it is 11.02's equation. Take 2x from both sides and subtract 18. Check in both sides of the first equation: 6 + 3 = 9 and 4 + 5 = 9.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.sub: Same steps, your numbers. Boards up when done.
slides.note: Quarters and sixths clear with 12: 12 times x/4 is 3x, 12 times −1 is −12, 12 times x/6 is 2x, 12 times 1 is 12. Take 2x: x − 12 = 12, so x = 24. Check: 6 − 1 = 5 and 4 + 1 = 5. A board with 3x − 1 = 2x + 1 multiplied only the fractions (x = 2); one with 24 as the multiplier is right too, with bigger numbers.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.note: Reveal; name what a wrong board most likely did (see the note above).

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 1 of 9
slides.note: Notes I's order with whole numbers. A board with x = 10/3 wrote 5x − 2 (the 5 to one term only); one with x = −2/3 wrote 5x + 10 (the sign). Check: 5(4) + 3 = 23 and 2(6) + 11 = 23.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 1 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 2 of 9
slides.note: Notes II with new numbers: −⅓ of 6x is −2x and −⅓ of −9 is +3. A board with x = −1 wrote −2x − 9 (the fraction to one term only); one with x = 1 wrote −2x − 3 (the sign). Check: −⅓(18 − 9) = −3 and 3 − 6 = −3.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 2 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 3 of 9
slides.note: Notes III and Example 1 with numbers that do not come out whole — the 21% skill at the state's level. 0.6 of 3x is 1.8x and 0.6 of 4 is 2.4. A board with x ≈ 1.83 wrote 1.8x + 4 (the decimal to one term only — the state's most common miss); one with x = 12.5 added the 2.4 (0.6x = 7.5). Check: 0.6(13.5 + 4) = 10.5 and 1.2(4.5) + 5.1 = 10.5.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 3 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 4 of 9
slides.note: Diagnostic, on a negative decimal factor (Notes III's kind). Option D is the sign, option C the one-term distribution, option B a term carried across the equals sign without its sign changing. On a split: sixty seconds to think again, re-vote — then check 5 in both sides: −1.5(10 − 6) = −6 and 5 − 11 = −6.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 4 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 5 of 9
slides.note: Example 2's move with new denominators: thirds and fifths clear with 15, and the 15 multiplies every term — the 1s as well. A board with x = 1 multiplied only the fractions (5x − 1 = 3x + 1); one stuck at 2x = 30 wrote the answer before dividing. Check: 15/3 − 1 = 4 and 15/5 + 1 = 4.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 5 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 6 of 9
slides.note: Diagnostic, and 11.03's endings with a fraction. Both sides are 3x − 2, so every number works. Option A distributed the 3 to one term and found 'no solution' — ask what 3 times −1 is. Options D and B read the true ending as an x — the same error, and the same reteach: say −2 = −2 aloud and ask for which x it is true. On a split: sixty seconds to think again, re-vote.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 6 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 7 of 9
slides.note: The extra-number board (ruling 22): Shop B's 3 blocks are not needed. Each shop's cost is an expression in h; they cost the same when the expressions are equal, 12 + 4.5h = 7.5h. Take 4.5h (the smaller) from both sides. Check: both cost \$30 for 4 hours.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 7 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 8 of 9
slides.note: Backwards: the solution is given and a number in the equation is missing. Put 2 in for x on BOTH sides — the right is 24, so 2 + □ must be 8. Check: 3(2 + 6) = 24 and 2(2) + 20 = 24.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 8 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 9 of 9
slides.sub: Take your time. Boards up when you have written it.
slides.note: Written, and the exit evidence. Read two aloud: one that distributes the 1.5 to both terms and checks in the first equation, and one whose check caught its own slip. The decimal is the 21% skill; the check is what proves the answer.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 9 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Independent Set
slides.sub: Six questions. On your own, in writing.
slides.note: Hand out the Independent Set; the same six questions are on the board. Silent work. Circulate and mark what you see; do not teach. Whatever is not finished goes home.

slides.title: IXL
slides.note: IXL: every listed skill is required, SmartScore 67. Due by the Unit 11 test.
